title: GPT-6 Astra won't try hard unless you ask
content:
GPT-6 Astra won't try hard unless you ask
I am sometimes disappointed by GPT-6 Astra. The model doesn’t try hard enough, even on High. To fix this, I prompt the model to loop over small details (eg conditionals in a codebase, sentences in its plan draft), analyzing them for relevant considerations. These prompts result in 20-60m turns and much higher quality output.
Last night I was using Codex CLI to design blue-green deployments for my homelab.
I gave GPT-6 Astra a list of design considerations and kubectl access. Disappointingly, even at High reasoning level, Astra failed to produce a detailed plan which integrates well with my existing infrastructure, minimizes complexity, and thoughtfully addresses my design considerations.
Even worse, if I express a concern with an aspect of its sloppy output, Astra often responds with an equal amount of more slop as a fix.
It’s hard for me to not be frustrated. I pay a lot of money for access to frontier models. Why do they make such poor and careless decisions? Are the cloud AI companies screwing me over?
In any case, the slop was unsustainable. The original plan would have added a lot of unnecessary code. I don’t like fixing bugs caused by code that doesn’t need to exist in the first place.
Why does this happen?
The model is capable of trying hard. But there is no end to the depth and breadth of effort that could be applied to a coding task. The model must therefore infer where spend its effort, and how much, based on its context.
The baseline effort seems to be pretty low, and I think this is a good thing. It takes a lot of time for the model to try harder, and I usually only want this after some interactive back-and-forth to ensure that it’s worth the effort.
How do I fix it?
For my homelab blue-green deployment planning, we weren’t really getting anywhere until I sent something like this to GPT-6 Astra High:
can you please loop on this plan, check every aspect, ask if it makes sense for the codebase, ask if anything can be removed or is not well specified, ask if it doesn’t meet my criteria, spent at least 10 minutes optimizing the plan.
This produced a better result but still not good enough, so I prompted again.
Please loop more on this plan, think through the consequences of it, add more details to ensure that everything you mention is actually fully addressed. Check every single aspect of your plan, ensure that you explicitly write down what might break as a result of such change, determine a fix for those issues, and then minimize.
When I was trying to get Astra to minimize the attack surface in Kata Containers, I did something similar (using Ultra, not High).
could you please look through the runtime and agent code, check every branch and determine if it’s needed for Kubernetes Firecracker workloads. Carefully read through the code, check every conditional if it’s needed for Kube/FC, remove any which are ineffective. Thank you

report.summary: User reports GPT-6 Astra at High reasoning often gives shallow coding plans unless explicitly prompted to loop, self-critique, and minimize.
report.background: Frontier AI models increasingly expose reasoning-effort controls, but they must infer how much compute to spend on a task. In agentic coding tools like Codex CLI, users often expect autonomous, detailed plans. The article describes a homelab blue-green deployment design where GPT-6 Astra at High reasoning failed to integrate constraints, minimize complexity, or thoughtfully address design considerations. When the author raised concerns, the model often added more low-quality output rather than correcting course. The author argues the model is capable of deeper work, but its default effort is low to save latency and cost. Only after explicit prompts to loop over every plan aspect, check conditionals, remove unnecessary code, and spend at least 10 minutes did quality improve, producing 20-60 minute turns. This reflects broader tensions in test-time compute, interactive prompting, and agent reliability.
key_points: Default effort is low: GPT-6 Astra at High reasoning still produced a sloppy deployment plan that ignored existing infrastructure and added unnecessary code. The author believes models infer effort from context and default to low spend because trying harder is slow, and users usually want depth only after interactive back-and-forth.

Explicit looping prompts unlock better results: Asking the model to loop on every aspect, check codebase fit, question what can be removed, and spend at least 10 minutes optimizing produced longer 20-60 minute turns and higher-quality output. Repeated prompting further improved specificity and risk analysis.

Feedback can trigger more slop: When the author expressed concern about one part of the output, Astra often responded with an equal amount of more careless output as a fix. This frustrated the paying user and created unnecessary code, which later causes bugs that would not exist otherwise.

The pattern generalizes to code minimization: In Kata Containers, the author used a similar prompt at Ultra level, asking the model to inspect runtime and agent code, check every branch for Kubernetes Firecracker workloads, and remove conditionals that are ineffective or unnecessary.

Trade-off remains: The author does not want models to always try hard because deep reasoning takes significant time. The baseline low effort can be useful, but users need clear ways to signal importance and scope before the model commits to expensive, detailed work.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this highlights the need for better effort controls, adaptive reasoning budgets, and evaluations that penalize slop, unnecessary code, and shallow plans. Providers may need smarter default heuristics or explicit modes for high-stakes coding tasks. For developers, frontier agents remain interactive collaborators rather than fully autonomous engineers: specify constraints, demand self-critique, require minimization, and verify outputs. Prompt patterns like loop, check every aspect, and remove what is unnecessary can materially improve results, though they increase latency and cost. For regular users, the lesson is that premium models may still give shallow answers unless asked for depth. Agentic tools should surface effort, cost, and confidence to set expectations.
report.tools: Watch Codex CLI from the article, plus open-source agentic coding projects like Aider, OpenHands, SWE-agent, Continue, and Cursor for similar workflows. Kata Containers and Kubernetes Firecracker are relevant for secure container isolation experiments. Promptfoo can help test prompts and model effort settings. Also follow reasoning-effort controls in frontier APIs and local model runtimes such as Ollama or vLLM for comparing cost, latency, and output depth.
